screens.title: Monitoring and Logging in a Fabric Network
screens.narratorSegment: In production, a Fabric network must be observable. In this lesson we focus on three pillars you will use daily: metrics collection, visualization, and centralized logging. You will learn which Fabric metrics matter for health and performance, how to use Prometheus to collect time-series data, how Grafana turns that data into dashboards, and how an ELK-based pipeline centralizes logs for search and audit. We also cover the built-in Fabric operational services that expose liveness and metrics endpoints used by scraping systems. Concrete examples will show how a Peer exposes a metrics endpoint and how a Prometheus scrape config identifies that endpoint. Why this matters: without instrumentation you cannot detect slow block commits, chaincode errors, or resource pressure until users are affected. A common misconception is that logging alone is enough — logs give rich detail but metrics give real-time behavior at scale. By the end of this lesson you will understand how these pieces fit together and why securing the UIs and endpoints is essential. Consider what metric you would monitor first in your network and why.

Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › Monitoring & Logging
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Monitoring and Logging in a Fabric Network

Understand the metrics Fabric exposes, how to collect them with Prometheus, visualize with Grafana, and centralize logs with the ELK stack. Learn how operational endpoints power health checks and why securing monitoring is critical.

In this lesson
Key metrics, Prometheus/Grafana, ELK pipeline, health endpoints, alerts and security practices.
Why it matters
Detect incidents early, trace failures, and meet audit requirements with searchable logs and dashboards.
Coming up
Hands-on Minikube walkthrough deploying Prometheus and Grafana to scrape a Fabric Peer.
Observability Stack
How metrics and logs align
Prometheus scrapes /metrics for time-series data.
Grafana visualizes and alerts from Prometheus sources.
ELK centralizes logs for search and forensic analysis.
Explore Key Topics
Prometheus Scraping
How Prometheus discovers and scrapes Fabric endpoints for metrics.
Grafana Dashboards
Import or build dashboards that highlight ledger height, latency, and chaincode invocations.
Centralized Logging
Ship Pod logs to Elasticsearch using Logstash or Fluentd and explore them in Kibana.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map to practical skills you will use to operate Fabric. First, you will identify which metrics matter: transaction rate, block commit latency, ledger height, and resource usage. Knowing these metrics helps you triage whether an issue is application-level or infrastructure-level. Second, you will implement Prometheus and Grafana to collect, store, and visualize metrics. This includes configuring Prometheus to scrape Fabric operational endpoints and building dashboards to surface trends. Third, you will configure centralized logging using the ELK stack or equivalent log shipper and storage so you can search errors and audit transactions. Finally, you will set up alerting so operators receive actionable notifications when thresholds are crossed. Each objective is tied to a verified competency milestone: you should be able to demonstrate a working scrape from a Peer, show a Grafana dashboard with Fabric metrics, and query recent chaincode error logs in Kibana. These are practical skills useful for maintaining uptime and performing incident response.

screens.title: Why monitoring and logging are essential
screens.narratorSegment: Operating a Fabric network without observability is risky. Monitoring supplies aggregated, real-time signals about throughput, latency, and resource usage; logging provides the narrative detail needed for debugging and compliance. For example, a spike in block commit latency may show up first as a degraded transaction rate in Prometheus metrics; logs from the peer or chaincode container will then explain whether the cause is a database slow query, chaincode exception, or C P U exhaustion. Metrics are optimized for alerting and trend analysis across many nodes; logs are optimized for deep, text-based forensic queries. A common misconception is that logs alone are enough — but logs are high-fidelity and verbose, making real-time analysis at scale difficult without time-series aggregation. Another pitfall is relying only on default retention: you must plan storage for Elasticsearch or Prometheus retention to support your investigation windows. In practice, combine both: use metrics to spot an anomaly and logs to investigate it. Think about a real incident you could detect using a commit-latency alert and then trace with chaincode logs. Why monitoring and logging are essential means monitoring gives real-time signals; logging provides detailed records for debugging and audit. both are required for reliable operations.. In practical terms, detect performance issues, security incidents, and maintain audit trails. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Monitoring gives real-time signals; logging provides detailed records for debugging and audit. Both are required for reliable operations.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › Why monitoring & logging
Definition & Role

Monitoring provides numerical measures over time; logging records events and context. Together they let you detect incidents, diagnose root causes, and provide audit trails for compliance.

Use metrics to detect anomalies quickly and trigger alerts.
Use logs to investigate and reproduce the sequence of events.
Plan retention and storage to keep relevant windows for investigations.
Concrete Example
Symptom
A drop in transaction throughput detected by Prometheus metrics.
Investigation
Query Kibana for ERROR logs from peer and chaincode containers around the incident timestamp.
Resolution
Identify a slow state database query in chaincode, optimize, and observe metrics recover.
Key Takeaway

Use metrics for fast detection and logs for deep analysis; both must be secured and retained appropriately.

screens.title: Fabric metrics you should monitor
screens.narratorSegment: Hyperledger Fabric components export a number of metrics that are meaningful for operations. Key signals include transaction processing rates, which tell you how many chaincode invocations are completing per second; block commit times, which indicate consensus and ordering latency; ledger height, which helps detect whether a peer has fallen behind; and state database query performance, which can reveal slow chaincode operations. Additionally, standard resource metrics like C P U, memory, and disk input and output from peers and orderers are critical to distinguish application bottlenecks from infrastructure pressure. For example, a rising commit time combined with high disk input and output suggests storage contention, whereas high C P U with normal disk input and output points to computation-heavy chaincode. A common misconception is that ledger height is sufficient to prove peer health — it shows progress but not latency or resource stress. Monitor multiple signals together and use Grafana dashboards to correlate them over time. Ask yourself: which two metrics would you check first when a user reports slow transactions? Fabric metrics you should monitor means watch throughput, commit latency, ledger height, state db latency, and resource usage to understand peer and orderer health.. In practical terms, transaction throughput, block commit latency, ledger height, state db performance, and resource utilization. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › Key Fabric Metrics
Primary Metrics to Monitor
Throughput
Transaction processing rate and chaincode invocation counters help detect load changes.
Commit latency
Time to commit blocks or transactions; rising values indicate ordering or endorsement delays.
Ledger height
Shows whether a peer is keeping up with latest blocks compared to other peers.
State DB performance
Query latency for CouchDB or LevelDB operations used by chaincode.
Quick Correlations
  • High commit latency + high disk I/O = likely storage contention.
  • High CPU + normal disk = compute-heavy chaincode or endorsement loops.
  • Falling ledger height = peer network partition or failed ordering connectivity.
Key Takeaway

Treat metrics as signals. Correlate multiple metrics to find real causes, not symptoms.

screens.title: Expose Fabric operational endpoints
screens.narratorSegment: Fabric exposes operational endpoints used for health checks and metrics. Each Peer and Orderer can run an operations service that listens on a configurable port and exposes endpoints such as a health check and a Prometheus-compatible metrics endpoint. To enable this, set the operations listen address and the metrics provider. For example, environment variables in a Peer container might set an operations listen address to enable the operations port and set the metrics provider to Prometheus. Once enabled, the Peer will serve metrics that include commit times, ledger height, and internal counters. A common mistake is forgetting to expose the operations port in the Pod spec or not configuring Prometheus discovery to look at that port. For Kubernetes, ensure the container ports include the operations port and that service selectors or pod annotations make the target discoverable by Prometheus. This step is essential because Prometheus relies on reachable HTTP endpoints to scrape metrics. In practice, verify with a simple HTTP GET to the health endpoint and confirm metrics are present at the metrics path. Expose Fabric operational endpoints means set the operations listen address and activate prometheus metrics on each peer and orderer to make metrics discoverable.. In practical terms, configure core_operations and metrics provider for peers and orderers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Enable operations
keyIdea.text: Set the operations listen address and activate Prometheus metrics on each Peer and Orderer to make metrics discoverable.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › Operations Service
Example environment snippet
# inside peer container spec
- name: CORE_OPERATIONS_LISTENADDRESS
  value: '0.0.0.0:9443' # enable operations service
- name: CORE_METRICS_PROVIDER
  value: 'prometheus' # enable Prometheus metrics
Also ensure the Pod exposes containerPort 9443 and Prometheus scrape configs target that port. Verify by querying the /healthz endpoint and checking the /metrics path for Prometheus-format metrics.
Checklist
  • Enable CORE_OPERATIONS_LISTENADDRESS on each Peer and Orderer.
  • Set CORE_METRICS_PROVIDER to prometheus.
  • Expose the operations port in the container spec and Service discovery.
  • Validate health and metrics endpoints before adding to Prometheus.
Key Takeaway

Operational endpoints must be enabled and reachable for scraping; missing them is a common root cause of empty metrics.

screens.title: Prometheus scraping configuration
screens.narratorSegment: Prometheus collects Fabric metrics by scraping HTTP endpoints. In Kubernetes, use pod discovery and relabeling rules to select only Pods that expose the operations port and have labels such as app=fabric-peer. The chapter provides a sample Prometheus config that illustrates a job for fabric-peer using kubernetes_sd_configs and relabel_configs to keep pods annotated for scraping and to map ports correctly. Important practical details: use annotations or labels to mark scrape targets, ensure the container port number matches the operations port, and use relabeling to construct the address with the correct port. A common misconfiguration is matching the wrong port or forgetting annotation keys, which results in no samples being collected. After applying a Prometheus config, verify targets in the Prometheus UI or query a known metric to ensure data flows. When working locally with Minikube, refer to the internal service DNS names for Grafana and Prometheus to configure data sources correctly. Prometheus scraping configuration means use kubernetes discovery, labels/annotations, and relabeling to reliably target fabric operations ports for prometheus scraping.. In practical terms, use kubernetes service discovery and relabeling to target fabric pods. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. keyIdea.title: Scrape Tips
keyIdea.text: Use Kubernetes discovery, labels/annotations, and relabeling to reliably target Fabric operations ports for Prometheus scraping.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › Prometheus Scrape Config
Excerpt: job for fabric-peer
job_name: 'fabric-peer'
kubernetes_sd_configs:
  - role: pod
relabel_configs:
  - source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_pod_label_app]
    action: keep
    regex: fabric-peer
  - source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_pod_container_port_number]
    action: keep
    regex: "9443"
  - source_labels: [__address__, __meta_kubernetes_pod_container_port_number]
    action: replace
    regex: ([^:]+)(?::\d+)?;(\d+)
    replacement: $1:$2
    target_label: __address__
This relabeling builds the correct address for scraping by combining Pod IP and container port.
Validation steps
  1. Confirm pods have app=fabric-peer label and expose port 9443.
  2. Apply Prometheus config and check Prometheus targets page for UP status.
  3. Query a known Fabric metric to verify samples arrive.
Common Mistake

Incorrect port selectors or missing annotations lead to zero scrape targets; always verify target discovery after deployment.

keyIdea.title: Deployment Steps
keyIdea.text: Deploy Prometheus and Grafana, configure Prometheus to scrape Fabric, and import a dashboard to visualize metrics locally.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › Local Deploy Flow
Prometheus manifest highlights
# Prometheus Deployment and ConfigMap
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: prometheus-config
data:
  prometheus.yml: |
    global:
      scrape_interval: 15s
    scrape_configs:
      - job_name: 'fabric-peer'
        kubernetes_sd_configs:
          - role: pod
        relabel_configs:
          - source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_pod_label_app]
            action: keep
            regex: fabric-peer
Apply the manifest with kubectl apply and ensure the Prometheus service is reachable by Grafana.
Grafana setup
Deploy Grafana, log in with the admin account, add Prometheus as a data source using the service name, and import a Fabric dashboard by ID. In Minikube use the service URL to access Grafana.
Try this

After import, confirm that fabric_peer_ledger_height appears and updates as blocks commit.

screens.title: Centralized logging with ELK
screens.narratorSegment: Centralized logging ensures you can search and analyze logs from all Fabric components in one place. The ELK stack is a common approach: use Logstash or Fluentd to collect Pod logs and forward them to Elasticsearch, which stores and indexes the logs, and use Kibana to search and create visualizations. In Kubernetes, log shippers run as DaemonSets or sidecars and parse container stdout/stderr into structured fields such as log level, container name, and timestamp. This structured indexing is what makes queries like "ERROR logs from peer0 between these timestamps" fast and reliable. Watch out for storage planning: Elasticsearch requires provisioned storage and tuning to handle retention. Another common mistake is shipping logs without parsing; raw logs are harder to query. For compliance or audit scenarios, ensure log retention meets policy and that access to Kibana and Elasticsearch is secured. A practical example: search Kibana for ERROR entries from a peer to trace a failed chaincode invocation and then cross-reference timestamps with Prometheus metrics. Centralized logging with ELK means ship pod logs to a central store, index them for search, and use kibana to analyze errors and audit events.. In practical terms, collect logs with logstash/fluentd and analyze with kibana. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Log shipping and parsing patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Log shippers take unstructured container logs and transform them into indexed documents suitable for search. Fluentd or Fluent Bit run as DaemonSets to collect logs from the node's container runtime, add metadata like namespace and pod name, and parse structured fields such as log level and JSON payloads emitted by chaincode. Logstash can be used when complex parsing and enrichment are required before indexing into Elasticsearch. Important operational patterns include adding Kubernetes metadata, parsing timestamps accurately, and tagging logs with component and severity. Also consider sampling verbose logs or using different indices for high-volume data to reduce pressure on Elasticsearch. A common mistake is forwarding raw logs without timestamp parsing, which breaks time-based queries. Another is not handling backpressure — configure buffering and retry policies in the shipper to avoid data loss. In practice, test your parsing rules with representative log samples and iterate so Kibana searches return precise results. screens.title: Alerting strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Alerting is how observability becomes actionable. Prometheus Alertmanager and Grafana both support alerts, but they play slightly different roles. Use Prometheus Alertmanager for metric-driven alerts that require complex routing, deduplication, and integrations like PagerDuty. Alertmanager is tightly coupled to Prometheus rules and excels at routing to on-call teams. Grafana also supports alerting based on dashboard panels and integrates well with notification channels for operator-facing dashboards. A practical approach is to implement production critical alerts in Prometheus Alertmanager and use Grafana alerts for dashboard-specific checks or temporary operational signals. Alert design matters: prefer simple, actionable alerts with clear runbooks. Avoid alert fatigue by using thresholds with hysteresis, grouping related alerts, and setting severity levels. A common misconception is that every metric needs an alert; instead focus on metrics that indicate user impact or risk, such as sustained high commit latency or peer availability loss. Always test alert delivery and escalation paths so alerts result in timely response. Alerting strategies means choose alertmanager for core, routed alerts and grafana for dashboard-centric checks; design alerts to be specific and actionable.. In practical terms, prometheus alertmanager vs grafana alerts — pick the right tool for the job. screens.title: Common mistakes and security considerations
screens.narratorSegment: Operators commonly run into a handful of repeatable mistakes when adding observability to a Fabric deployment. First, missing metrics endpoints: forgetting to enable the operations service or to set the metrics provider results in no data to scrape. Second, incorrect scrape configurations: wrong service names, ports, or label selectors prevent Prometheus from discovering targets. Third, insufficient log retention or storage: Elasticsearch requires provisioned storage and lifecycle policies; otherwise logs may be deleted before you can investigate incidents. Fourth, lack of alerting: it is not sufficient to collect data — you must surface issues with actionable alerts. Fifth, security gaps: exposing Prometheus, Grafana, or Kibana UIs without authentication or network controls can leak sensitive operational data. Mitigations include enabling operations endpoints correctly, validating Prometheus targets post-deploy, planning storage and retention for logs, configuring Alertmanager or Grafana alerts, and securing UIs with authentication and network policies. These practices prevent common operational blind spots and harden observability tooling. Common mistakes and security considerations means enable endpoints correctly, verify scraping, plan log retention, set alerts, and secure dashboards to avoid operational blind spots.. In practical terms, avoid missing endpoints, misconfigured scrapes, retention issues, and unsecured dashboards. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Summarizing three core ideas will help you retain what matters. First, Prometheus is a pull-based monitoring system that scrapes metrics endpoints to collect time-series data; it is the primary way to gather Fabric metrics for real-time alerts and historical trends. Second, Grafana is the visualization layer that connects to Prometheus and turns raw metrics into dashboards and alerts that operators use to assess health and performance. Third, the ELK stack centralizes logs: Logstash or Fluentd forwards logs to Elasticsearch where Kibana enables search and forensic analysis. Together these three components form a complete observability strategy: metrics for fast detection, dashboards for situational awareness, and centralized logs for deep investigation. Keep in mind the practical requirements: enable Fabric's operations service, configure Prometheus discovery properly, plan storage for logs, and secure the monitoring UIs. These combined practices give you sightlines into your Fabric network so you can detect, investigate, and respond to incidents.

fullNarratorScript:
In production, a Fabric network must be observable. In this lesson we focus on three pillars you will use daily: metrics collection, visualization, and centralized logging. You will learn which Fabric metrics matter for health and performance, how to use Prometheus to collect time-series data, how Grafana turns that data into dashboards, and how an ELK-based pipeline centralizes logs for search and audit. We also cover the built-in Fabric operational services that expose liveness and metrics endpoints used by scraping systems. Concrete examples will show how a Peer exposes a metrics endpoint and how a Prometheus scrape config identifies that endpoint. Why this matters: without instrumentation you cannot detect slow block commits, chaincode errors, or resource pressure until users are affected. A common misconception is that logging alone is enough — logs give rich detail but metrics give real-time behavior at scale. By the end of this lesson you will understand how these pieces fit together and why securing the UIs and endpoints is essential. Consider what metric you would monitor first in your network and why.

These objectives map to practical skills you will use to operate Fabric. First, you will identify which metrics matter: transaction rate, block commit latency, ledger height, and resource usage. Knowing these metrics helps you triage whether an issue is application-level or infrastructure-level. Second, you will implement Prometheus and Grafana to collect, store, and visualize metrics. This includes configuring Prometheus to scrape Fabric operational endpoints and building dashboards to surface trends. Third, you will configure centralized logging using the ELK stack or equivalent log shipper and storage so you can search errors and audit transactions. Finally, you will set up alerting so operators receive actionable notifications when thresholds are crossed. Each objective is tied to a verified competency milestone: you should be able to demonstrate a working scrape from a Peer, show a Grafana dashboard with Fabric metrics, and query recent chaincode error logs in Kibana. These are practical skills useful for maintaining uptime and performing incident response.

This second objectives screen ties the skills to verification steps and practical scope. You will be able to point Prometheus at a running Fabric Peer and show a successful scrape of its metrics endpoint. You will import or build Grafana dashboards that display fabric_peer_ledger_height and chaincode invocation counters. You will demonstrate log collection by querying Elasticsearch or Kibana for ERROR level entries produced by a Peer or chaincode container. Finally, you will configure alerting rules for key thresholds and verify delivery through an integration such as email or a messaging channel. Each objective emphasizes reproducible, demonstrable outcomes: a working scrape, a dashboard with at least three Fabric metrics, a searchable log query that returns recent errors, and an alert that fires under a test condition. These are the operational competencies you can use to prove readiness for production responsibility.

Operating a Fabric network without observability is risky. Monitoring supplies aggregated, real-time signals about throughput, latency, and resource usage; logging provides the narrative detail needed for debugging and compliance. For example, a spike in block commit latency may show up first as a degraded transaction rate in Prometheus metrics; logs from the peer or chaincode container will then explain whether the cause is a database slow query, chaincode exception, or C P U exhaustion. Metrics are optimized for alerting and trend analysis across many nodes; logs are optimized for deep, text-based forensic queries. A common misconception is that logs alone are enough — but logs are high-fidelity and verbose, making real-time analysis at scale difficult without time-series aggregation. Another pitfall is relying only on default retention: you must plan storage for Elasticsearch or Prometheus retention to support your investigation windows. In practice, combine both: use metrics to spot an anomaly and logs to investigate it. Think about a real incident you could detect using a commit-latency alert and then trace with chaincode logs. Why monitoring and logging are essential means monitoring gives real-time signals; logging provides detailed records for debugging and audit. both are required for reliable operations.. In practical terms, detect performance issues, security incidents, and maintain audit trails. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Hyperledger Fabric components export a number of metrics that are meaningful for operations. Key signals include transaction processing rates, which tell you how many chaincode invocations are completing per second; block commit times, which indicate consensus and ordering latency; ledger height, which helps detect whether a peer has fallen behind; and state database query performance, which can reveal slow chaincode operations. Additionally, standard resource metrics like C P U, memory, and disk input and output from peers and orderers are critical to distinguish application bottlenecks from infrastructure pressure. For example, a rising commit time combined with high disk input and output suggests storage contention, whereas high C P U with normal disk input and output points to computation-heavy chaincode. A common misconception is that ledger height is sufficient to prove peer health — it shows progress but not latency or resource stress. Monitor multiple signals together and use Grafana dashboards to correlate them over time. Ask yourself: which two metrics would you check first when a user reports slow transactions? Fabric metrics you should monitor means watch throughput, commit latency, ledger height, state db latency, and resource usage to understand peer and orderer health.. In practical terms, transaction throughput, block commit latency, ledger height, state db performance, and resource utilization. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Fabric exposes operational endpoints used for health checks and metrics. Each Peer and Orderer can run an operations service that listens on a configurable port and exposes endpoints such as a health check and a Prometheus-compatible metrics endpoint. To enable this, set the operations listen address and the metrics provider. For example, environment variables in a Peer container might set an operations listen address to enable the operations port and set the metrics provider to Prometheus. Once enabled, the Peer will serve metrics that include commit times, ledger height, and internal counters. A common mistake is forgetting to expose the operations port in the Pod spec or not configuring Prometheus discovery to look at that port. For Kubernetes, ensure the container ports include the operations port and that service selectors or pod annotations make the target discoverable by Prometheus. This step is essential because Prometheus relies on reachable HTTP endpoints to scrape metrics. In practice, verify with a simple HTTP GET to the health endpoint and confirm metrics are present at the metrics path. Expose Fabric operational endpoints means set the operations listen address and activate prometheus metrics on each peer and orderer to make metrics discoverable.. In practical terms, configure core_operations and metrics provider for peers and orderers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Prometheus collects Fabric metrics by scraping HTTP endpoints. In Kubernetes, use pod discovery and relabeling rules to select only Pods that expose the operations port and have labels such as app=fabric-peer. The chapter provides a sample Prometheus config that illustrates a job for fabric-peer using kubernetes_sd_configs and relabel_configs to keep pods annotated for scraping and to map ports correctly. Important practical details: use annotations or labels to mark scrape targets, ensure the container port number matches the operations port, and use relabeling to construct the address with the correct port. A common misconfiguration is matching the wrong port or forgetting annotation keys, which results in no samples being collected. After applying a Prometheus config, verify targets in the Prometheus UI or query a known metric to ensure data flows. When working locally with Minikube, refer to the internal service DNS names for Grafana and Prometheus to configure data sources correctly. Prometheus scraping configuration means use kubernetes discovery, labels/annotations, and relabeling to reliably target fabric operations ports for prometheus scraping.. In practical terms, use kubernetes service discovery and relabeling to target fabric pods. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The Prometheus ConfigMap should include a scrape job that selects fabric-peer pods. After Prometheus is running, deploy Grafana, log into the UI, and add Prometheus as a data source pointing to the Prometheus service. Import a Fabric dashboard to visualize metrics. In Minikube, services can be exposed using NodePort or the Minikube service command to obtain a URL. The chapter provides example manifests for Prometheus and Grafana. Key operational notes: use a ServiceAccount and RBAC rules to allow Prometheus to discover pods, and prefer a persistent volume for Grafana storage in production. For validation, import a dashboard and check that metrics such as fabric_peer_ledger_height and fabric_peer_chaincode_invocations_total populate graphs. This hands-on flow is the foundation for building production-grade dashboards later. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Centralized logging ensures you can search and analyze logs from all Fabric components in one place. The ELK stack is a common approach: use Logstash or Fluentd to collect Pod logs and forward them to Elasticsearch, which stores and indexes the logs, and use Kibana to search and create visualizations. In Kubernetes, log shippers run as DaemonSets or sidecars and parse container stdout/stderr into structured fields such as log level, container name, and timestamp. This structured indexing is what makes queries like "ERROR logs from peer0 between these timestamps" fast and reliable. For compliance or audit scenarios, ensure log retention meets policy and that access to Kibana and Elasticsearch is secured. Log shippers take unstructured container logs and transform them into indexed documents suitable for search. Fluentd or Fluent Bit run as DaemonSets to collect logs from the node's container runtime, add metadata like namespace and pod name, and parse structured fields such as log level and JSON payloads emitted by chaincode. Logstash can be used when complex parsing and enrichment are required before indexing into Elasticsearch. Important operational patterns include adding Kubernetes metadata, parsing timestamps accurately, and tagging logs with component and severity. Also consider sampling verbose logs or using different indices for high-volume data to reduce pressure on Elasticsearch. A common mistake is forwarding raw logs without timestamp parsing, which breaks time-based queries. Another is not handling backpressure — configure buffering and retry policies in the shipper to avoid data loss. In practice, test your parsing rules with representative log samples and iterate so Kibana searches return precise results. Alerting is how observability becomes actionable. Prometheus Alertmanager and Grafana both support alerts, but they play slightly different roles. Use Prometheus Alertmanager for metric-driven alerts that require complex routing, deduplication, and integrations like PagerDuty. Alertmanager is tightly coupled to Prometheus rules and excels at routing to on-call teams. Grafana also supports alerting based on dashboard panels and integrates well with notification channels for operator-facing dashboards. A practical approach is to implement production critical alerts in Prometheus Alertmanager and use Grafana alerts for dashboard-specific checks or temporary operational signals. Alert design matters: prefer simple, actionable alerts with clear runbooks. Avoid alert fatigue by using thresholds with hysteresis, grouping related alerts, and setting severity levels. A common misconception is that every metric needs an alert; instead focus on metrics that indicate user impact or risk, such as sustained high commit latency or peer availability loss. Always test alert delivery and escalation paths so alerts result in timely response. Alerting strategies means choose alertmanager for core, routed alerts and grafana for dashboard-centric checks; design alerts to be specific and actionable.. In practical terms, prometheus alertmanager vs grafana alerts — pick the right tool for the job. Operators commonly run into a handful of repeatable mistakes when adding observability to a Fabric deployment. First, missing metrics endpoints: forgetting to enable the operations service or to set the metrics provider results in no data to scrape. Second, incorrect scrape configurations: wrong service names, ports, or label selectors prevent Prometheus from discovering targets. Third, insufficient log retention or storage: Elasticsearch requires provisioned storage and lifecycle policies; otherwise logs may be deleted before you can investigate incidents. Fourth, lack of alerting: it is not sufficient to collect data — you must surface issues with actionable alerts. Fifth, security gaps: exposing Prometheus, Grafana, or Kibana UIs without authentication or network controls can leak sensitive operational data. Mitigations include enabling operations endpoints correctly, validating Prometheus targets post-deploy, planning storage and retention for logs, configuring Alertmanager or Grafana alerts, and securing UIs with authentication and network policies. These practices prevent common operational blind spots and harden observability tooling. Summarizing three core ideas will help you retain what matters. First, Prometheus is a pull-based monitoring system that scrapes metrics endpoints to collect time-series data; it is the primary way to gather Fabric metrics for real-time alerts and historical trends. Second, Grafana is the visualization layer that connects to Prometheus and turns raw metrics into dashboards and alerts that operators use to assess health and performance. Third, the ELK stack centralizes logs: Logstash or Fluentd forwards logs to Elasticsearch where Kibana enables search and forensic analysis. Together these three components form a complete observability strategy: metrics for fast detection, dashboards for situational awareness, and centralized logs for deep investigation. Keep in mind the practical requirements: enable Fabric's operations service, configure Prometheus discovery properly, plan storage for logs, and secure the monitoring UIs. These combined practices give you sightlines into your Fabric network so you can detect, investigate, and respond to incidents.

Keep three compact reminders at hand as you operate Fabric. First, always enable and verify the operations service and Prometheus metrics provider on each Peer and Orderer so your monitoring can actually collect data. Second, correlate metrics and logs: metrics surface anomalies quickly and logs let you diagnose root causes. Third, secure and plan: protect dashboards and endpoints with authentication, and provision adequate storage and retention for logs and metrics to support investigation windows. These checks are simple but often overlooked. Before you declare a network observable, confirm a working scrape, a Grafana dashboard updating with Fabric metrics, and a log query in Kibana that returns recent ERROR entries. Those three verifications are the minimum for production readiness.
